hypothesis: The neuron responds strongly to close-up, high-definition views of eyes or eye-like features embedded within dense, organic textures. The core activating visual element is a distinct circular or almond-shaped form containing a high-contrast internal structure: typically a dark black pupil surrounded by a colored iris (often amber, yellow, or brown) and punctuated by a sharp, bright white specular highlight. This feature is consistently framed by high-frequency, fibrous, or patterned textures such as animal fur, concentric feather rings, or mottled skin, which often flow around or radiate from the eye. The dominant colors are warm, natural earth tones—including golden-tan, russet, beige, grey, and creamy white—which contrast with the deep black of the pupil and the glossy reflectivity of the eye surface. The face or textured body region typically fills 60–100% of the image frame, with the eye itself serving as a focal point positioned centrally or slightly off-center. The neuron is invariant to the specific biological identity (dog, owl, human, or marine life) and lighting conditions, provided the sharp structural definition of the eye and the surrounding organic texture are preserved.
